On top is Cristiano Ronaldo, next to Jorge Jesus, and below is Homelander, with the same sideways glance and the same half-smile of someone who has just been contradicted and is calculating how much longer he can stand to stay quiet.
That's what the internet sees in the two of them: the most powerful man in the room who can't handle a "no."

Homelander flies, brings down planes and shoots lasers out of his eyes, but he loses control the moment someone decides something for him, and Cristiano, who in twenty years won everything a player can win, spent the last four fighting with every coach, club and executive who dared to tell him he would have to wait his turn.

On November fifth, twenty twenty-six, Cristiano Ronaldo announced that he would no longer play for the Portugal national team, five weeks after walking out of the camp in the middle of an international break, having fallen out with the coach he himself had recommended for the job.

The greatest goalscorer in the history of international football said goodbye without a farewell match, reading a letter in a phone video, and to understand how the story got to this point, we have to go back four years in time.

For those who have never seen the series, Homelander is the strongest superhero on the planet: he flies, shoots lasers out of his eyes, is practically indestructible and has his face on every poster in the United States.

But The Boys shows what happens when the cameras turn off, and there he is a man who needs to be adored all the time, who can't stand sharing the stage with anyone and who, when someone takes the spotlight away from him, reacts like a child who lost his toy, with the difference that this child can bring down an airplane.
What's frightening about the character is realizing that no power in the world solves the one thing he can't stand, which is no longer being the center.
And anyone who takes a calm look at Cristiano Ronaldo's last four years will see that same weakness showing up again and again, harder and harder to hide.
The first time the world saw it clearly was on an October night in twenty twenty-two, at Old Trafford.

Manchester United were beating Tottenham two-nil, in one of their best performances of that season, and Cristiano, who had returned to the club a year earlier as the prodigal son, was watching it all from the bench.
In the final minutes, when Erik ten Hag wanted to bring him on, Ronaldo refused, got up and walked down the tunnel before the final whistle, leaving his teammates to celebrate without him.
Three weeks later, he was sitting in front of Piers Morgan saying that he felt betrayed by the club and that he didn't respect the manager, and within a few days his contract was terminated.
In the third season of The Boys, the company that runs the heroes decides that Homelander will share the leadership of the group with Starlight, the heroine the public has come to love more than him.
He smiles for the cameras, accepts the announcement and spends the rest of the season working to make it fail, because for this kind of character, being second in line hurts more than any defeat.

Four years later, in October twenty twenty-six, Ten Hag spoke about that period again in an interview with The Athletic and used a line worth remembering, because it will come back before the end of this video: he said that Ronaldo let the team down and let him down, because the two of them had made plans together.
From England, Cristiano went to Saudi Arabia, where he would have what he always wanted, an entire league revolving around him, and for three years that is exactly what happened.

Until, in the January twenty twenty-six window, Al Hilal, Al Nassr's biggest rival, signed Karim Benzema, and Cristiano concluded that the fund that controls the country's four biggest clubs was placing its bets somewhere else.
His answer was to stop playing.

He sat out three games in a row, with no injury and no physical problem, in open protest against the fund, while the league sent harsh messages through the press and a Saudi TV host pointed out that no Manchester City player would refuse to take the field to protest against the club's owner.
A week later, he came back as if nothing had happened.

In the second season of the series, something very similar happens: a new heroine joins the group, starts growing on social media, the company starts betting on her, and the most powerful man in the world behaves like someone who has just been replaced by a newer model.
On the eve of the game against Ireland, in November twenty twenty-five, Cristiano told reporters that he really liked the Irish fans and promised to behave.

The next day, with Portugal losing two-nil at the Aviva Stadium, he looked at an Irish defender and made the gesture of someone wiping away imaginary tears, and a few minutes later he spun around and landed an elbow on Dara O'Shea's back.
The referee showed yellow, VAR called him over and the yellow became red, the first of his career in two hundred and twenty-six games for his country.
On his way to the tunnel, while fifty thousand people threw the crying gesture back at him, Cristiano stopped, looked up at the stands, applauded ironically and raised both thumbs.
At the end of the third season of The Boys, Homelander loses control in front of a crowd and does the worst possible thing, and the crowd applauds.
In Dublin, the crowd did the opposite: they filmed, laughed and imitated.
That was when a lot of people realized that the hero's smile was looking more and more like the villain's sneer.

In the fourth season of the series, Homelander's best-kept secret is a small detail: he is going gray.
He secretly plucks out the white hairs and has his hair dyed, because the hero who sells himself as eternal cannot be seen getting old.
Cristiano built his entire career on his body, and in twenty twenty-six, at forty-one, the body began to collect.
In February, a thigh injury took him off the pitch three months before the World Cup.

In June, in the opener against DR Congo, in Houston, Portugal drew one-all, he spent the game unable to make an impact, heard the opposing fans chant Messi's name and earned a new nickname on social media: Homelando, his name mixed with Homelander's.
The body still had a few flashes left.
He scored two goals in a five-nil rout of Uzbekistan and, against Croatia, finally scored the first goal of his career in a World Cup knockout game.
But in the round of sixteen, Spain won with a Merino goal in stoppage time, and his last World Cup ended with Cristiano crying on the pitch in Dallas.
The nickname, which was supposed to last a week, stuck.

After the World Cup, the Portuguese federation hired Jorge Jesus, the same coach Cristiano had brought to Al Nassr and who, according to the player himself, he recommended to the federation's president.
In August, the two of them sat down and agreed on a plan: in the September international window, Cristiano would play the first and the last match.
In the first game, against Wales, he started, came off in the second half and, before leaving the pitch, put the captain's armband on Bruno Fernandes's arm with his own hands.
On the day of the game in Norway, Jesus called Cristiano over at lunchtime and asked if he could handle thirty minutes, and he said yes.
He warmed up from halftime, watched the clock run, watched João Félix and Gonçalo Ramos score the winning goals and didn't come on.
At the end, he left the pitch without acknowledging the fans.
Two days later there was a meeting, and this is where the story gets too similar to the series.

According to the statement Cristiano himself published later, it was agreed that Jesus would open the press conference by reading points from a text approved by the player, and one of those points said that the coach had been wrong to have someone of the stature of Pelé or Maradona warm up and not come on.

He said at the press conference that the one who decides who plays is the coach, and an hour later Cristiano left the camp in Copenhagen and wrote on Instagram that, in due time, he would tell everyone the truth.
In The Boys, the one who writes what Homelander says in public is the company, and the whole series is about the day he decides he doesn't need a script anymore.
In real life, it went the other way around: it was the hero who was writing the script for the coach to read.
The federation suspended Cristiano for thirty days and fined him two hundred and fifty-five euros, which for him is a symbolic amount, but which put on paper what had happened.
José Mourinho, who coached Cristiano at Real Madrid, went public to say that he needed to adapt to a new phase of his career.
A day after the suspension, Ten Hag's interview came out, the same one from the beginning of this video, with that line about the plans made together.
Two coaches, separated by four years and two countries, said they had planned with Cristiano, left Cristiano on the bench and watched Cristiano walk away.
At the end of The Boys, Homelander loses his powers and, in front of the cameras, humiliates himself begging for his own life, while the people who adored him turn off the television in disgust.
The series ends with him having no control over how he would be remembered.
The letter Cristiano read on November fifth goes in the opposite direction.

In it, he admits that he also failed, thanks kit men and physiotherapists who never appeared in the photos and writes that no captain walks alone, which is perhaps the strangest sentence to hear from someone who spent the last four years walking alone out of every place where he wasn't the center.
He still plays for Al Nassr and is still chasing the thousandth goal of his career, so the story isn't over.
But the last image left of him in a Portugal shirt wasn't a goal or a trophy: it was that man with his arms crossed on the bench in Oslo, the same image the internet put next to Homelander.
Homelander never found out who he was when he stopped being the strongest in the room.
Cristiano Ronaldo, at forty-one, still has the chance the character never had.
